DRO seeks a model that performs well regardless of the perturbation: inff supQ∈U Ex∼Q[ℓf(x)]. The induced robustness can directly imply generalization: if the data that forms ˆ Pn is drawn from a population distribution P, and U is large enough to contain P, then we implicitly optimize for P too and the DRO objective value upper bounds out of sample performance. In machine learning, the DRO uncertainty set U has so far always been deﬁned as a φ-divergence ball or Wasserstein ball around the empirical distribution ˆ Pn. These choices are convenient, due to a number of structural results. For instance, the performance of MMD is highly sensitive to bandwidth selection [2,22,23]; the unprojected Wasserstein distance suffers from slow finite-sample convergence; projected Wasserstein methods are sensitive to hyperparameter choices (such as kernel type, regularization, and projection dimension), rely on nonconvex optimization without global optimality guarantees, and are computationally expensive [41]; and edge-count graph-based tests may lose power under scale alternatives or become unstable when sample sizes are unbalanced [11,12]. We compare against Box's M [7], Energy distance [37], SMAI [32], MMD (Gaussian kernel) [22], Ball Divergence (BD) [35], Kernel Projected Wasserstein (KPW) [41], and a graph-based two-sample test (gTest) [11]. Since the one-dimensional Wasserstein (1DW) distance has a closed-form expression, given by the absolute difference between the quantile functions of the compared distributions, we leverage quantile approximation techniques for sample streams to define the streaming 1DW distance. We obtain an estimate for the expected subspace robust Wasserstein distance between any probability measure on the unit ball of a separable Hilbert space, and its empirical distribution from n i.i.d. samples.

# Using Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) to Compare Kernel Density Estimates (KDEs). I'm interested in comparing two `Kernel Density Estimates (KDEs)` and I've come across the `Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD)` metric as a potential method for doing so. Can MMD be used to compare KDEs? If so, what considerations should I be aware of when using MMD to compare KDEs I appreciate any insights, advice, or examples that can help me better understand and apply MMD in the context of comparing KDEs. edited Feb 13, 2024 at 2:27. **Can MMD be used to compare KDEs?**. Yes, the MMD metric can be used to compare KDEs. MMD is a distance measure between distributions and is defined as the distance between their embeddings in the Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Space (RKHS) . The MMD can be used to construct statistical tests to determine if two samples are drawn from different distributions, making it applicable for comparing KDEs . **Considerations when using MMD to compare KDEs**. When using MMD to compare KDEs, there are several considerations to be aware of:. * **Choice of Kernel Function**: The choice of kernel function used in the MMD calculation can impact the results. Different kernel functions can be used, and the selection should be based on the specific characteristics of the data being compared . * **Bandwidth Selection**: The bandwidth parameter used in the kernel density estimation can affect the performance of MMD. * **Sample Size**: The sample size used for estimating the KDEs can influence the MMD calculation. Larger sample sizes can lead to more accurate estimates of the MMD. * **Interpretation of Results**: It's crucial to interpret the results of the MMD comparison in the context of the specific problem or application. Understanding the implications of the MMD values in relation to the compared KDEs is essential for drawing meaningful conclusions . By considering these factors, the MMD metric can be effectively utilized to compare Kernel Density Estimates and provide insights into the differences between distributions. results.title: [PDF] A Kernel Two-Sample Test | Semantic Scholar
results.content: # A Kernel Two-Sample Test. title={A Kernel Two-Sample Test},. This work proposes a framework for analyzing and comparing distributions, which is used to construct statistical tests to determine if two samples are drawn from different distributions, and presents two distribution free tests based on large deviation bounds for the maximum mean discrepancy (MMD). This paper proposes a method to boost the power of the kernel test by combining MMD estimates over multiple kernels using their Mahalanobis distance and derives the asymptotic null distribution of the proposed test statistic and uses a multiplier bootstrap approach to efficiently compute the rejection region. A new one-sample test for normality in a Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Space that test the null-hypothesis of belonging to a given family of Gaussian distributions is proposed, based on the same principle as the MMD which is usually used for two-sample tests such as homogeneity or independence testing.

results.content:
Title: confidence interval - Why would I want to bootstrap when computing an independent sample t-test? (how to justify, interpret, and report a bootstrapped t-test) - Cross Validated
# Why would I want to bootstrap when computing an independent sample t-test? First, I am a little confused about the normality assumption of the t-test, which might be why I am not totally getting bootstrapping. Is the assumption for the t-test that (A) the data is sampled from a normal population, or (B) that your sample distributions have Gaussian properties? I can bootstrap to see if my sample is normal, right? So, one reason you would bootstrap is to be more certain of the normality of your sample data, correct? Do people not perform a t-test on the bootstrapped samples? Bootstrap actually fairs quite poorly for small sample sizes, even when the population is normal. Both the t-test and the bootstrap are based on sampling distributions, what the distribution of the test statistic is. The t-test happens to be fairly robust to the normality assumption (as far as the size of the test goes, power and precision can be another matter) so for some cases the combination of "Normal enough" and "Large sample size" means that the sampling distribution is "close enough" to normal that the t-test is a reasonable choice. The bootstrap instead of assuming a normal population, uses the sample CDF as an estimate of the population and computes/estimates (usually through simulation) the true sampling distribution (which may be normalish, but does not need to be). The disadvantage of the bootstrap is that it is very dependent on the sample representing population because it does not have the advantages of other assumptions. The bootstrap does not give you normality, it gives you the sampling distribution (which sometimes looks normal, but still works when it is not) without needing the assumptions about the population. If you do not have normality and do have small samples, then neither the t-test or the bootstrap should be trusted. With huge sample sizes the large sample theory will benefit both t-tests and bootstrapping and you will see little or no difference when comparing means. With moderate sample sizes the bootstrap can perform well and may be preferred when you are unwilling to make the assumptions needed for the t-test procedures.
